title: AI Is Quietly Changing Who Gets to Build Software
author: Marc Watkins
summary: Marc Watkins argues that AI coding agents are quietly transferring the power to build educational software away from EdTech vendors and toward individual teachers and professors, who can now use natural language to build bespoke tools rather than buying pre-packaged products. He offers three concrete examples — a searchable database of prize-winning nonfiction, a side-by-side Homer reading tool with original Greek and multiple translations, and his own anatomy-comparison workshop for Allied Health students — as evidence that faculty-built AI code can be a deliberate response to 'AI slop' rather than a capitulation to it. But he tempers the optimism with two warnings: citing Amelia Wattenberger, he notes that heavy reliance on AI coding agents can make building feel 'voyeuristic,' watching a machine work rather than staying grounded in the process; and he flags that AI detection is already a losing arms race, since students can cheaply run their own writing through an AI coding agent against a detector's API until it passes. The piece closes on an equity argument specific to K-12: because Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google are giving free premium AI access to K-12 teachers, a high-school teacher in the poorest district may now have better-resourced AI tools than a professor at a wealthy university, even as K-12 districts and colleges take opposite approaches to mandating versus permitting AI use in the classroom.
points: Watkins's central claim is structural, not just pedagogical: AI coding agents let subject-matter experts (a historian, a literature professor, a health-sciences instructor) build their own learning tools directly, which threatens EdTech vendors' traditional monopoly on making educational software.

His three case studies (Breen's nonfiction database, Boyer's Homer Reader, his own Anatomy Atelier) are offered as proof that faculty-built AI tools can be intentionally anti-'AI slop' — built to slow readers down and sharpen critical judgment rather than offload thinking.

Citing Amelia Wattenberger, Watkins warns that heavy AI-coding reliance risks making the builder 'voyeuristic' — watching the machine work rather than staying present in the making — a caution against uncritical adoption even by AI's advocates.

The equity argument is the piece's sharpest point: because Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google are giving free premium AI access specifically to K-12 teachers, a teacher in the poorest U.S. school district may now out-resource a professor at an elite, wealthy university.

Watkins flags that AI-detection tools are already circumventable for a few dollars a month (via repeated rewrites against a detector's own API), arguing that policy alone — without faculty AI fluency — is 'an incomplete response.'
quotes: Frontier models can be amazingly proficient in one category (coding) and completely unimpressive in many others (writing, social reasoning, etc.). Knowing the difference matters.

Breen used a combination of OpenAI's GPT 5.6 and Claude's Fable to create a searchable database of prize-winning and nominated nonfiction. Breen argues that reading quality non-fiction books are the antithesis of AI slop, but it has become really hard to find exceptional writing authored by human beings.
Using AI code, we no longer have to rely on a vendor to provide us with a digital product. We can now create those experiences, edit them, take ownership of them, and respond in real time.
Tasking Codex or Claude Code to complete a project is increasingly voyeuristic—you watch a machine do the work and wait for it to finish.
For a few dollars a month, anyone can task their AI coding agent to rewrite text hundreds of times, testing it against Pangram's classifier until it passes detection.

A high school teacher working in the poorest district in the United States has greater access to premium AI tools, coupled with data protection, than a professor working at some of the wealthier universities.

While some K12 districts have started mandating teachers use AI tools in their classrooms, no college campus has been so instructive or intrusive to telling its faculty to do so, leaving individual instructors to decide what response to AI in their class is appropriate.
